business_rules.value: Unknown: which documents or classifications may be edited after signature, what a manager may change, whether prior signatures are invalidated or re-collected, and whether a manager may approve their own edit.

challenges.headline: 'Edit' a signed document
challenges.premise: The request says managers will edit documents after they are signed, as if the signed document itself changes.
challenges.alternative: Treat every post-signature change as a new version that supersedes the signed one. The signed version stays frozen and referenceable, and the edit happens only on the successor draft. This is my reasoning from the document model, where prior signatures and citations point at a specific version.
challenges.consequence: A true in-place edit would break the link between a signature and the content it covered, and would leave signed content altered without a trace. That is a compliance and legal exposure, and retrofitting an audit trail later is expensive.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'create a new version', and that signed content is never overwritten, before any design starts.

challenges.headline: Managers as editors and approvers
challenges.premise: Managers both make the edit and drive its re-approval, as the request phrases it, without saying who actually approves.
challenges.alternative: Separate the right to propose a change from the right to approve it, so the editing manager cannot approve their own successor version. The approver can be drawn from the existing circuit or a different one.
challenges.consequence: If the editor can also approve, a signed document can be changed and re-validated by one person. That defeats the purpose of re-approval and is hard to defend at audit.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client who approves a successor version, and whether the original signatories must sign again, before building the circuit.

challenges.headline: Is a new build needed?
challenges.premise: Post-signature editing is assumed to be a missing capability that must be built.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has versioning, approval circuits and e-signature. The need may be met by exposing 'new version from a signed document' through those existing pieces, with a few rules on top, rather than building a separate engine.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel mechanism would duplicate approval and versioning logic, and would drift from the existing audit and classification behaviour.
challenges.recommendation: Check how signed documents are changed today and what the existing versioning and circuits already do, then scope only the gap.

challenges.headline: Editing signed documents at all
challenges.premise: Managers should be able to 'edit' a signed document and then re-approve it, as if the signed document were a working draft.
challenges.alternative: Treat every change as a new version that supersedes the signed original. The original stays untouched and referenceable, and the manager edits a copy. Separately, a lighter path for pure corrections (typos, formatting) and a full path for changes to terms could be offered, because the two carry different legal weight.
challenges.consequence: If 'edit' means changing a signed version in place, prior signatures no longer correspond to the content and the audit trail loses its meaning. A single flow for both a typo and a change of terms either over-burdens trivial fixes or under-controls substantive ones.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client that signed versions are never modified. Ask them to sort their real post-signature changes into trivial corrections and substantive changes, then decide whether those get different controls.

challenges.headline: Re-approval is enough
challenges.premise: The request says 'edit and re-approve' and does not mention signatures, implying that approval of the new content restores the document's standing.
challenges.alternative: Decide explicitly, per document type, whether the new version needs fresh signatures from the original signatories, or whether an approval by the right circuit is sufficient. This is my reading of the request: it is silent on signatures, and I have not assumed either answer.
challenges.consequence: If signatures are required and the build only delivers approval, the resulting documents may not carry the legal value people assume. If approval is enough, the build is much smaller. The two answers are different builds.
challenges.recommendation: Get a written answer from the client's legal or compliance owner on whether a superseding version needs new signatures before estimating.

challenges.headline: Any manager, any signed document
challenges.premise: Managers are the right group to start changes on signed documents, with no limit stated on which documents or which managers.
challenges.alternative: Limit the right to document owners or to the manager of the relevant area, and limit by document type and confidentiality level. Re-approval by someone other than the editing manager separates the person who changes from the person who approves.
challenges.consequence: Broad edit rights on signed documents widen exposure to unauthorised changes and complicate audits. Access in this platform is driven by classification, so a permissive rule can expose restricted documents through new versions, search and notifications.
challenges.recommendation: Propose owner-scoped rights with classification limits as the starting point, and confirm who re-approves before building the circuit.

challenges.headline: Editing signed documents literally
challenges.premise: Managers can 'edit' a document once it has been signed, and re-approval follows.
challenges.alternative: Treat the request as issuing a new version (or an amendment, for contracts) and leave the signed version frozen. A signature then always points at the exact content it was given for, and no one has to explain a signed document that quietly changed.
challenges.consequence: If 'edit' means in-place change, the original signatures no longer match the content, the audit trail loses its evidential value, and anything citing the signed version silently points at different text. If it means a new version, the build is much larger than an edit form: re-signature, supersession and history.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client, before any estimate, that they mean a new version with the original retained. Ask which change they actually need to make (typo, changed terms, corrected data), since that decides the rest.

challenges.headline: Managers as sole editors
challenges.premise: Managers are the right people to change signed content and to re-approve their own changes.
challenges.alternative: Let a manager initiate the change, but route re-approval to someone other than the author (the original approvers or a higher level), so the person who edits is not the one who validates. This is a proposal; the client has not named a re-approver.
challenges.consequence: If the editing manager can also approve, a signed document can be changed with no independent check, which undermines the point of having signed it. Allowing any manager to edit any signed document also widens access beyond what classification and ownership would normally allow.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client who re-approves and who must re-sign, and whether editing rights are limited to the document owner or department.

challenges.headline: Building before checking reuse
challenges.premise: A new capability is needed for post-signature changes.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has versioning, approval circuits and, for contracts, an amendment flow with its own draft-to-issued lifecycle. Part or all of the request may be met by exposing these to managers, rather than building a new mechanism.
challenges.consequence: Building a separate flow duplicates the approval and versioning logic and creates two ways to change a signed document, with diverging rules and audit behaviour.
challenges.recommendation: Map the request against the existing versioning, approval and amendment features first, and only build the gap.

complexity_reasons: supersession with retained history and re-signature
multi-step re-approval circuit with an independent approver
the approved vs published vs current distinction
audit trail that must have no gaps
briefs.cost_driver: supersession of signed versions with re-signature and audit
risks: People may act on a superseded or not-yet-re-approved version if 'current' is not defined clearly.
Signatories may be unaware a signed document was changed, or prior signatures may be treated as still valid for new content, creating legal exposure.
Anything that references the old version (links, citations, earlier signatures) must be reconciled, or it silently points at the wrong text.
Access and classification rules touch search, listings, notifications and export, so a permission change here ripples across shared modules.
Regulatory position (signature validity, retention, audit) is not yet established, so scope could grow late.

opportunities.text: Reuse the existing versioning and approval circuit for supersession instead of building a separate flow, so one mechanism covers every post-signature change.
Generalise the contract amendment pattern (draft to issued, re-opens signature) into a shared 'supersede a frozen version' capability for all document types.
Make the audit trail of version changes a shared service that also serves retention and access reporting.

next_steps: Hold a short session with the client to confirm that 'edit' means a new version with the signed original retained, and to learn which changes they actually need to make.
Map the request against the existing versioning, approval and amendment features to identify the real gap before estimating.
Settle who re-approves, who re-signs and who may start a change, as the basis for the permission and circuit design.
Define what 'current' means while a new version is pending, and then estimate the build, including the audit trail.

decisions.decision: A signed version is never changed in place; a change creates a new version and the original is retained.
decisions.why: Signatures and citations point at a specific version, and the audit trail must stay reliable.
decisions.alternative: Overwrite the signed document and keep the original signatures valid.
decisions.tradeoff: A larger build (re-signature, supersession, history) in exchange for signature validity and audit integrity.

decisions.decision: Re-approval uses the platform's existing multi-step approval circuit.
A full audit trail covers every change to a signed document.
decisions.why: The edit targets signed content, so who changed what and who re-approved must be provable.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra build effort in exchange for defensibility at audit.
